Compare Historical PMMS Results Frequently Asked Questions Toggle all accordion sections Expand All What data is used for PMMS? The PMMS results are based on data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA): mortgage rates collected from thousands of loan applications submitted to Freddie Mac from lenders across the country when a borrower applies for a mortgage. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . How is the national average determined? We collect the mortgage rate of all purchase applications based on PMMS criteria and a national average mortgage rate is calculated out of all the selected loan applications. The criteria include weekly conventional, single-family originations with conforming loan limits as set by FHFA. Is the PMMS rate based on current lender quotes or recent settlements? PMMS rates are based on applications submitted to Freddie Mac for the given week from lenders across the country. What type of lenders are included in the PMMS? Currently, our lenders are a mix of credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies. Do the PMMS results represent the rates charged on a specific day of the week? If so, which day? Or are they the average rate charged that week? PMMS is published each Thursday at noon ET. When a U.S. holiday falls on a Thursday, the PMMS will publish on the Wednesday of that week. The week of application activity starts at 12:00 a.m. ET the prior Thursday and lasts through 11:59 p.m. ET Wednesday. Therefore, the PMMS results are an average of loan rates offered Thursday through Wednesday. See our publication calendar . Why are adjustable rates no longer published? ARMs indexed to alternatives to U.S. Treasury securities have become more prevalent in the market. As we worked on enhancing the PMMS , we carefully considered which loan products were most popular for the PMMS borrower profile (good/excellent credit, 20% loans, home purchase loans on owner occupied 1-unit single-family properties). Additionally, in recent years the mortgage market has been dominated by fixed mortgage products. While there has been an uptick recently in the share of adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) for the broader mortgage market, ARMs remain most popular for higher loan size (nonconforming) loans. Why are fees/points no longer published? Under the current LPA requirements, fees and points are not always required to be provided by lenders. Therefore, we are not able to report on the average fees and points. How has PMMS changed over time? Since April 1971, Freddie Mac shared the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate with the PMMS. We have updated the information we collect and the process for gathering data over time. Changes in Data Processes When it was launched, PMMS surveyed lenders on the rates and points for their most popular 30-year fixed-rate, 15-year fixed-rate and 5/1 hybrid amortizing adjustable-rate mortgage products. The survey was based on first-lien prime conventional conforming home purchase mortgages with a loan-to-value of 80 percent. In addition, the adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) products were indexed to U.S. Treasury yields, and lenders were asked for both the initial coupon rate and points as well as the margin on the ARM products. Lenders surveyed each week were a mix of lender types — credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies — roughly proportional to the level of mortgage business that each type commands nationwide. On November 17, 2022, the mortgage rate gathering process was updated. Instead of surveying lenders, we now use data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA). Changes in Information Shared In 1984 , the 1-year ARM was added to the survey. In 1991 , the 15-year fixed-rate mortgage rate was added. In January 2005 , a 5/1 hybrid ARM series was added. In January 2016 , the 1-year ARM was discontinued. In November 2022 , adjustable rates and fees/points were discontinued. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . items.title: Anthropic's Record IPO Reverberates Across Data Center Sector
items.description: Anthropic raised $81.3B in the largest-ever stock market debut Thursday, briefly driving the Claude maker’s valuation north of $2T and delivering a vote of confidence for an artificial intelligence infrastructure boom that has faced growing scrutiny from investors. Wikimedia Commons/TechCrunch Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei in 2023 Shares began trading on the Nasdaq Stock Market at $111.50 and climbed as high as $114.99 midday Thursday before dipping back below $100 — but still well above the company’s $83 offering price and the $70-to-$78 range Anthropic had anticipated earlier this month. The debut surpasses the previous initial public offering record set by rival AI firm SpaceX in June. The offering comes at a turbulent moment for the AI trade and the data center and digital infrastructure sector supporting it. Investors have grown increasingly uneasy about the staggering sums tech giants are spending to fund an infrastructure construction boom that has yet to generate commensurate returns. Rising community opposition and political headwinds in the wake of this month’s midterm elections have added another layer of uncertainty. The anxiety has been felt in public markets, with several companies tied closely to the AI data center boom delaying planned IPOs in recent weeks amid concerns about valuations and investor appetite for AI. Anthropic's debut may provide a counterpoint to that narrative and a direct boost to the data center sector. The IPO gives one of the world’s largest AI labs a massive pool of capital, a significant portion of which will flow toward computing capacity and data centers. Bryn Talkington, managing partner of Requisite Capital Management, told CNBC on Thursday that Anthropic becoming a public company also provides transparency into a major demand driver for digital infrastructure that has previously been lacking. This could give investors confidence that tech’s AI infrastructure spending spree will deliver returns. “This raise solidifies the capex spend,” Talkington said. “Now you have a real player that’s not being marked up by VC companies. You have a real player — SEC, quarterly earnings — and that creates transparency and accountability, which I think is a wonderful thing.” Anthropic’s move to the public markets coincides with a strategic shift that is expected to make the firm a major player in the data center landscape. In its S-1 prospectus filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission in October, Anthropic disclosed plans to reduce its reliance on cloud providers by leasing dedicated data centers at significant scale and operating its own computing hardware inside them. The strategy marks a departure for a company that has previously relied almost entirely on cloud providers like Amazon , Google and Microsoft for its computing power. Through the initiative, Anthropic Direct, leased data centers under Anthropic’s control will account for a growing share of the $542B to $567B the company plans to spend on computing infrastructure in the coming years, it said in the S-1 filing. Anthropic doesn't intend to develop data centers itself. Third-party providers will secure land and power, build facilities to Anthropic’s specifications and operate them on its behalf. The initiative is already moving beyond the planning stage, with Anthropic entering into purchase and lease agreements for Anthropic Direct, according to its SEC filing. “As our compute requirements have scaled, we have transitioned to a hybrid model in which, in addition to purchasing compute as a cloud service, we also procure specialized AI accelerators directly and operate this hardware in dedicated data center facilities leased and operated on our behalf, to our specification,” the company wrote in its SEC filing. But the company also said in its SEC filing that challenges building data centers will present a risk for the company, and the headwinds facing data center development have only increased since. November’s midterms saw voters across the U.S. approve local moratoriums and other measures to restrict data center development, while elections in key markets like Texas and Georgia produced new governors and other state officials who campaigned on limiting data centers. Democratic control of both chambers of Congress is also expected to bring greater scrutiny for the industry. Speaking with CNBC on Thursday morning, Anthropic President Daniela Amodei said the company will prioritize local input in its data center build-out to ensure communities don’t feel that the technology “is happening to them.” She also said the company is committed to paying for any increases in the cost of grid power that may occur due to the firm’s data centers. “From our perspective, building data centers is something where we also need to listen to what it is that those communities want and help to bring forward that future as well,” she said, adding that the company is aiming to “make sure that any cost increase is not borne by the consumer.” Continue reading this story with a free account Log in or register Related Topics: Anthropic , Artificial Intelligence , Claude , Dario Amodei , NASDAQ

items.description: U.S. Retail Monthly Foot Traffic & Sales Analysis | October 2026 Nov 19, 2026 Colliers Retail Market Intelligence October retail spending surges as early holiday shopping fuels sales and traffic growth. Download Report Experts Nicole Larson Senior Manager, National Retail Research | U.S. Anjee Solanki National Director, Retail Services & Practice Groups Summary Analysis U.S. retail sales maintained strong momentum in October, rising 6.9% year over year while foot traffic increased 1.6%. Core retail sales grew 5.5%, with underlying volumes increasing 2.8%, signaling stronger consumer demand as the holiday shopping quarter began. Gas station sales surged 30.1%, contributing to overall sales growth, while early holiday promotions helped lift non-store sales by 10.1%. Apparel continued to attract shoppers seeking value and seasonal purchases. Apparel sales increased 4.9%, with underlying volumes rising 1.2% as consumers favored discounted mid- and premium-priced merchandise. Clothing foot traffic climbed 6.4%, while department store visits jumped 11.3%, highlighting strong in-store engagement ahead of the holidays. Electronics spending remained strong, with sales increasing 7.6% despite a 3.4% decline in store visits. Product innovation and replacement demand helped support spending, even as consumers became more selective about where and how they shop. Furniture and furnishings sales rose 2.2%, with foot traffic increasing 2.1%, suggesting gradual improvement in home-related spending despite ongoing housing market challenges. Experiences and hobbies continued to draw consumers. Theater and music venue visits surged 28.5%, attractions increased 11.4%, and hobbies, gifts and crafts traffic climbed 17.9%. Meanwhile, grocery sales grew just 1.2%, with underlying volumes declining 0.5%, reflecting continued pressure on household budgets and a shift toward value-oriented shopping channels. Top-performing brands include Five Below, Ross Dress for Less, Barnes & Noble, Ollie's Bargain Outlet, BJ's Wholesale Club, Nordstrom Rack, Dollar Tree, Grocery Outlet, Carter's & OshKosh B'gosh, and Total Wine & More. Download the full October report for deeper insights into category-level performance, consumer spending behavior and the retailers driving traffic growth across the U.S. retail market. items.title: Office Development Hits 10-Year Low as Demand for Top Space Climbs
items.description: National CRE News In Your Inbox. Sign up for Connect emails to stay informed with CRE stories that are 150 words or less. National + Weekender | November 19, 2026 By: Amy Wolff Sorter Office Development Hits 10-Year Low as Demand for Top Space Climbs Sandy Romero, Cushman & Wakefield Not so long ago, there was too much office supply and not enough vacancy. Then, there’s now. Cushman & Wakefield’s Global Office Supply report said that global office development is at its lowest level in a decade. With 580 million square feet under construction during Q3 2026, “the under-construction pipeline is 45% below its Q3 2017 peak of 1.04 billion square feet,” the report said. Meanwhile, in the United States, space under construction is at 23 million square feet, down 83% from its 2020 high. At the same time, “occupiers keep gravitating to high-quality, amenitized buildings, and that space is being absorbed faster than it can be replaced. That is pushing Class A vacancy down and supporting rent growth,” Sandy Romero, head of office & alternatives, global research at Cushman & Wakefield , told Connect CRE. It’s All About the Money Quite simply, the slowdown in construction and deliveries is because “building costs have risen faster than consumer prices,” the report explained. Supply chain disruptions, energy and shipping cost shocks, and labor shortages are among the reasons. Additionally, U.S. base rates stood at 3.75% in the third quarter, with further increases expected into early 2027. To assess whether new projects make financial sense, Cushman & Wakefield relied on economic rent, the minimum rent a new office building must earn to be profitable. Economic rent combines land acquisition costs, construction, operational expenses, leasing, developer margins and borrowing costs incurred during the development. On average, North American market rents were about 6% below economic rents. But those rents vary by city. New York, NY: Market rents of $156.64 per square foot are nearly 60% above economic rent of $98.69. About 6.4 million square feet were under construction as of the third quarter, nearly double the level of a year earlier. More than 2.5 million square feet is also under renovation as owners respond to tenants’ push for better space. Miami, FL: Class A starting rents are up 39% over three years, and Class A vacancy is 16%, down 180 basis points from a year ago. The pipeline of 1.8 million square feet is nearly three times last year’s level. “Among the metros, Miami is already there,” Romero said. Dallas, TX: Romero said that class A vacancy fell nearly 230 basis points (bps) over the past year to 26.3%, while starting rents are up 36% over three years. She expects build-to-suit and renovation projects to lead in the near term. “If vacancy keeps tightening, speculative projects could start to be planned in the next couple of years,” she added. Boston, MA: Market rents averaged $78.59 per square foot in 2026, 8% below economic rent of $85.38. No projects are under construction or renovation. Market rents are projected to rise above economic rent in 2029, driven by strong demand for newer Class A space. San Francisco, CA: Market rents of $98.43 per square foot are just 4% below economic rent of $102.94, the narrowest gap among markets still below the break-even point. Class A vacancy remains high at 31.1%, while the pipeline has been empty for almost four years. Chicago, IL: Chicago has the widest gap. Market rents of $84.56 per square foot are 10% below, meaning new construction isn’t likely to make financial sense until 2032. Los Angeles, CA: Romero said Los Angeles is furthest from the break-even point. Class A vacancy averaged 25.8% in the third quarter. “Class A starting rents are up 16% over three years, but that hasn’t kept pace with construction costs and other pressures,” Romero observed. Another potential quandary is federal fund rate hikes. However, Romero pointed out that such increases count but aren’t a deciding factor in development. “The economic rent needed to justify a project does include the cost of capital, and an additional hike could push out viability timelines modestly,” she explained. “But rent growth is the bigger lever, since demand for top-tier space is already lifting rents.” Class B and—Oversupply? The word “oversupply” can send jitters throughout the commercial real estate sector. It’s also an interesting term for office construction. Romero said that despite issues such as the doubling of construction in places like New York City, overbuilding won’t be an issue in the current cycle. “New York’s inventory shrunk by 1.6% over the past three years,” she explained. “Annual completions have averaged 1.8 million square feet, about 45% below the 10-year average of 3.2 million.” Additionally, rents and demand are high enough to support new development. There is also plenty of Class B space, but that’s not a cure-all for demand. Romero said that value-seeking tenants could take on the older, less fancy space. “However, tenants looking for highly amenitized space for their workforce won’t see Class B as a substitute,” she commented. Owners wishing to compete would need to upgrade to Class A standards, where the building allows. “Where it doesn’t, they may face prolonged vacancy or benefit from conversion to another use,” Romero said. The Recommendations Building an office is more capital intensive than ever. How can all parties determine when such a project actually pencils? For investors : The report suggested that investors target markets with strong fundamentals, including locations with emerging or severe supply shortages where demand far outweighs new deliveries. For developers : Look for any edge in capital or development costs, secure skilled labor before the project starts to avoid delays and consider distressed sales that generate a redevelopment strategy. items.title: Anthropic’s Blockbuster IPO Set To Spark a New San Francisco Housing Frenzy: ‘Expect More All-Cash Offers’ and Bidding Wars
items.description: Real estate agents in San Francisco are bracing for further acceleration of the housing market as Anthropic makes an initial public offering at a reported valuation of $1.5 trillion. The Bay Area has been a hot spot for newly wealthy AI trendsetters in recent years, rebuilding a market that was left hurting during the COVID-19 pandemic as tech offices emptied. With major AI companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic planting roots in San Francisco, the housing market has grown competitive, leading what some real estate agents are calling a “ mansion shortage .” Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO went live on Thursday, marking one of the largest public-market debuts in history. The Claude developer, which will trade under the ticker ANT, initially said it planned to price shares at between $70 and $78, which would value the company at between $1.3 trillion and $1.45 trillion. Late Wednesday, The Wall Street Journal reported the company planned to debut at $83 per share, taking the valuation to $1.5 trillion. In addition to the public offering, Anthropic is set to receive an extra $26 billion in a private placement sale of shares to several other major tech companies, including Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, and more, according to Yahoo Finance . While employees and insiders won't see cash in hand until after a significant lockup period, the debut could give many early shareholders the confidence to move forward with real estate purchases. “Confidence may change before purchasing power does. There are lockup periods, taxes, and individual circumstances to consider, so I wouldn’t expect everyone to start buying houses the following week,” San Francisco real estate agent and founder of Vivre Real Estate , Danielle Lazier , tells Realtor.com® . “But the anticipation has already motivated some buyers to act because they’re concerned about competing with more AI money later.” This will not be the first IPO debut that Lazier has worked through, so she knows how the influx of confidence and wealth can push people toward real estate investments. Even tech companies that hit major milestones without going public can lead to major shifts in local spending. “Having worked here through Google, Facebook, and other IPOs, I’ve seen how that wealth can move into housing as people diversify and make longer-term plans,” says Lazier. “OpenAI hasn’t gone public, but its private stock sales have already helped employees buy homes.” Loading... Jason Henry/Bloomberg via Getty Images AI cash already transforming Bay Area real estate The AI boom has already significantly reshaped the housing market in the Bay Area . Realtor.com research found that elevated down payments in the Bay Area, when compared to key comparison markets like Miami, New York City, and Austin, TX, are evidence of the impact of AI wealth. The study captured baseline down payment numbers from 2020 to 2022, when AI hadn’t yet taken hold and mortgage rates hadn’t spiked. When mortgage rates peaked in 2023 and buyers put more money down if able, down payments within the luxury home market rose between 3 and 8 percentage points in all four metros. In the 2024–25 period, mortgage rates had eased, but the AI boom was in full swing. Down payments in Miami, New York City, and Austin all met or dropped below their pre-rate-shock level, but buyers in the Bay Area continued to put 6.6 percentage points more down to buy a home, showing clear evidence that AI equity had found its way into pockets and into real estate. By 2026, the median down payment in counties considered to be AI hubs, including San Francisco, Santa Clara, and San Mateo, reached 25%, while median down payment in nearby nonhub counties of Alameda, Contra Costa, and Marin remained at 20%. When applied to the AI-hub group’s median listing price of about $1.33 million, that 5-percentage-point difference translates to $61,180 in additional down payment, according to Realtor.com data. Loading... San Francisco has long been impacted by tech booms, including the development of Facebook and Google. Realtor.com research has made a significant connection between the recent AI boom and increased down payments throughout the Bay Area. David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images The influx of new wealth has been compounded by a limited number of desirable homes, making the market fiercely competitive. “Additional purchasing power is competing for a limited resource. We have very few spacious, finished homes with practical layouts in desirable location,” says Lazier. “Having the money to renovate doesn’t mean having the time or interest to manage a San Francisco construction project.” Homes with completed renovations, outdoor space, views, and privacy draw the most interest. Lazier mentions that she expects listings like 2770 Broadway , which hit the market last week as the city’s most expensive listing of 2026, to be ones to watch. The stunning seven-bedroom, 6.5-bathroom home hits all the marks: a beautiful view of the San Francisco Bay, a sport court in the back, and a 2007 renovation that combines its classic architecture with functional modern living. It also comes with a $35 million asking price. Loading... The newly wealthy are discerning homebuyers, and not everyone will be going after estates with flashy price tags. items.title: Why housing construction is sliding back toward COVID-era lows
items.description: The great housing construction boom that people have been cheering about for four years now looks to be on the cusp of falling to COVID-era lows. How is this possible when people have been saying for the past five years that we need to build more homes and Congress just passed the giant ROAD to Housing Act this summer — which was designed to help spur more construction. The old laws of economics still play out here; there simply isn’t enough housing demand to build more homes. This is something I wrote about back in June 2021 : when mortgage rates eventually rise this whole thing will reverse. Now, in November 2026, we are not that far away from the COVID-19 recession lows, as housing permits are already at COVID-19 recession levels and mortgage rates are above 7%. Building permits From Census : Building Permits: Privately-owned housing units authorized by building permits in October were at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1,295,000. This is 7.4 percent below the revised September rate of 1,398,000 and is 8.7 percent below the October 2025 rate of 1,418,000. Single-family authorizations in October were at a rate of 772,000; this is 8.7 percent below the revised September figure of 846,000. Authorizations of units in buildings with five units or more were at a rate of 475,000 in October. As we can see in the chart below, housing permits have been slowly falling for years and we are not only at levels last seen during the COVID-19 recession, but we’re on pace to hit the lows of that time period if this trend continues. And all this is happening when mortgage rates are close to 7.5% and the Fed is starting a new rate hike cycle. Single-family permits are not only close to the lows of 2022, but not that far from the COVID-19 recession lows either. Builders have done an admirable job keeping new home sales elevated enough to keep housing starts from falling further, but that has limits as profit margins fall. As you can see here, the single-family permits have taken a noticeable dive. Builders confidence at multiyear lows One question I got recently, which has merit: Why is builder confidence at multiyear lows, but new home sales have grown over the last few months? Just remember that the builder confidence index is tilted toward smaller homebuilders, not the big publicly traded homebuilders that are still buying down rates to move product. New home sales are still at 2019 levels, and so are housing starts and permits. If the big builders lose their ability to buy down rates, this sales data should eventually break below 2019 levels, but for now sales have operated within a small range for the past 10 years. Conclusion Since mortgage rates shot toward 7.60%, we have seen housing data turn very negative. Compare that to last year at this time, when mortgage rates were heading toward 6% and existing home sales hit a nine-month high. The big builders can only do so much to keep starts from falling more. For now, it doesn’t look good for housing construction in 2027, given where mortgage rates are at and the builders profit margins falling more and more. Related More:

How is this possible when people have been saying for the past five years that we need to build more homes and Congress just passed the giant ROAD to Housing Act this summer — which was designed to help spur more construction.
The old laws of economics still play out here; there simply isn’t enough housing demand to build more homes.
This is something I wrote about back in June 2021 : when mortgage rates eventually rise this whole thing will reverse.

items.title: Home Purchase Loans Fall to Lowest Third-Quarter Level Since 2012
items.description: Home Purchase Loans Fall to Lowest Third-Quarter Level Since 2012 by ATTOM Team | Nov 19, 2026 | Mortgage Origination , Real Estate News - Recent Articles Home purchase lending falls 9 percent quarter-over-quarter to 729,968 loans; Refinance lending drops 16 percent quarter-over-quarter to 561,290 loans IRVINE, Calif. – Nov. 19, 2026 — ATTOM , the leading provider of property data , AI-powered intelligence , and real estate analytics solutions, today released its U.S. Residential Property Mortgage Origination Report for the third quarter of 2026, showing purchase and refinance lending slowed from the previous quarter as mortgage rates climbed and home purchase loans fell to their lowest third-quarter level since 2012. A total of 1.29 million purchase and refinance mortgages secured by residential property (1 to 4 units) were originated in the third quarter, down 12 percent from the previous quarter and 15 percent from a year earlier. Total loan volume reached $498.1 billion, down 15 percent quarterly and 12 percent year-over-year. The quarterly slowdown was driven by declines in both home purchase and refinance lending. Purchase loans fell 9 percent from the previous quarter to 729,968, marking the lowest third-quarter total since 2012. Purchase loans were down 12 percent from a year earlier, even as the average purchase loan amount rose 3 percent over the same period to $411,756. “The increase in refinance activity we saw late last year and into early this year cooled in the third quarter, with refinancing declining more than purchase lending,” said Rob Barber, CEO of ATTOM. “Purchase loans also slipped to their lowest third-quarter level since 2012, as higher mortgage rates and elevated average purchase loan amounts continued to strain affordability for many buyers.” Purchase lending slips quarterly in most markets Purchase lending totaled $300.6 billion in the third quarter, down 10 percent from the previous quarter and 10 percent below year-ago levels. Purchase loans accounted for 56.5 percent of all purchase and refinance originations, up from 54.5 percent in both the second quarter of 2026 and the third quarter of 2025. Purchase activity declined quarterly in 73.6 percent of analyzed metro areas with a population of 200,000 or more and sufficient data. Among metros with populations above 1 million, the largest quarterly increases were in Buffalo, NY (up 61 percent); Memphis, TN (up 50 percent); Rochester, NY (up 32 percent); New York, NY (up 22 percent); and Hartford, CT (up 20 percent). The steepest quarterly drops among large metros were in Salt Lake City, UT; New Orleans, LA; Denver, CO; Atlanta, GA; and Richmond, VA. Refinancing activity falls sharply quarter-over-quarter Refinancing activity fell 16 percent quarter-over-quarter to 561,290 loans, the lowest quarterly total since the second quarter of 2024, and was 19 percent below the third quarter of 2025. Refinance originations accounted for 43.5 percent of all purchase and refinance loans, down from 45.5 percent in both the previous quarter and a year earlier. Refinance lending declined quarterly in 89.4 percent of analyzed metro areas, with the steepest quarterly drops among large metros in San Jose, CA; Dallas, TX; San Francisco, CA; Austin, TX; and Louisville, KY. FHA and VA loan shares decline quarterly Loans backed by the Federal Housing Administration accounted for 15.7 percent of all purchase and refinance originations in the third quarter, down from 16.1 percent in the second quarter and 17.9 percent a year earlier. VA-backed loans represented 6.9 percent of originations, down from 8.2 percent in the second quarter and 7.2 percent a year earlier, the lowest share since the second quarter of 2024. Mortgage rates climb above 7 percent by early October Mortgage rates trended higher during the quarter. According to Freddie Mac, the average rate on a 30-year fixed mortgage rose from 6.43 percent in early July to 7.28 percent by early October, adding pressure to an already constrained housing market. NYC Capital Markets: Volume Moderates but Remains on Track for Recovery Year After four quarters of sustained recovery, investment sales slowed in the third quarter. Dollar volume totaled $5.6 billion, a 30.7% quarter-over-quarter (QOQ) decline and the first quarter since Q2 2025 to fall short of at least $8.0 billion. Investor confidence, which had steadily improved over the last year, was tempered by rising interest rates, uncertainty around the broader economy and geopolitical conditions, and the historically consistent trend of an election cycle pause. Despite the slowdown, the year-to-date (YTD) dollar volume total of $22.0 billion remains virtually unchanged from the same period last year, while the year’s annualized pace of $29.3 billion would represent a 23.3% increase over the 2020 cyclical low. In Q3 2026, there were 517 transactions involving the sale of 578 properties—an 18.2% year-over-year (YOY) decrease in properties sold. Average pricing for core property types across New York City fell to $504 per square foot (psf), a 0.6% decrease from the 2025 average. Cap rates for core property types have continued to inch higher in 2026 and now stand at an average of 7.13%. Sector Highlights Office: Dollar volume in Q3 2026 dipped to $1.4 billion, bringing the YTD total to $5.5 billion, only 7.8% below the same period last year. Although activity remains muted compared to historical levels, the investor pool is steadily expanding, with deals this quarter completed by a diverse mix of institutional, REIT, private capital, and user-purchasers. The average deal size declined for the third consecutive quarter, to $46.8 million, as smaller private capital players deployed more capital into value-add strategies for discounted and underutilized assets. At the same time, larger investors remain attracted to well-positioned, sizeable Class A assets with favorable tenancy and capital improvement conditions. Pricing has declined nominally this year, down 4.2% to $478 psf. Multifamily: Although combined dollar volume for elevator and walk-up properties slowed to $1.1 billion in Q3 2026, the YTD total of $4.8 billion falls only 11.7% short of the total from the same period last year, which marked the strongest year since 2022. Similar to the office sector, multifamily demand is starkly bifurcated between market-rate, newly-constructed, often luxury assets versus majority-rent-regulated, deeply discounted offerings—though both segments are exhibiting encouraging momentum. Substantial renter demand has kept vacancy at historic lows and attracted a growing pool of capital from both core/core-plus investors as well as value-add players. Development: Volume pulled back slightly to $831.6 million in Q3 2026, but the sector remains on pace to finish at $5.0 billion: if achieved, 2026 and 2025 would be the only two years since 2019 to surpass that benchmark. Depressed land values and a still-limited supply pipeline continued to drive activity. That momentum, previously focused in Manhattan, has begun to spread to the city’s secondary markets: four out of the five largest development transactions this quarter were located in the Outer Boroughs, totaling $249.6 million across 1.3 million buildable square feet. Increased demand has continued to support pricing recovery, with the citywide price per buildable square foot rising 6.4% YOY to $227, the highest average since 2019. items.title: Another Small Victory For Mortgage Rates
items.description: Another Small Victory For Mortgage Rates By: Matthew Graham 1 Hour, 13 Min ago The present week continues to be rather uneventful for mortgage rates , although not at all unpleasant. It began with Monday largely holding in line with Friday's latest levels. While those were the highest in several weeks, we've made slow and steady progress since then. Each of the past 3 days has resulted in modest improvement with today's installment being the smallest so far at only 0.01%. The only caveat is that rates have needed some help in order to keep this gentle progress intact. A vast majority of "help" since early-to-mid October has come in the form of a stock market correction and general concerns over the sustainability of the AI boom. This has resulted in bond yields frequently correlating with major stock market averages like the NASDAQ or S&P. Today was no exception. Bonds were slightly weaker at first (thus implying slightly higher mortgage rates). It wasn't until stocks began to swoon around 10am ET that bond yields dropped, thus allowing mortgage lenders to set today's rates a bit lower than they otherwise could have. items.description: Monthly Housing Payments Fell to Lowest Level in Nearly 2 Months–But Rates Are Climbing Again Published on November 19th, 2026 by Dana Anderson Home prices are slipping and house hunters have more room to negotiate. But mortgage rates that are going back up could make the math harder for would-be buyers. What to know about the U.S. housing market for the four weeks ending November 15: Home-sale prices edged down for the fourth week in a row. The median home-sale price was $388,516, down 0.4% year over year. That extends a streak that followed three years of increases. Monthly housing payments dropped to their lowest level in nearly 2 months. The median monthly mortgage payment was $2,723 at a 7.11% mortgage rate, the weekly average. This data is seasonally adjusted. Payments are down from $2,760 a week earlier but still up 8.2% from a year ago. The relief may not last: the daily average mortgage rate rose to the 7.5% range this week. Homebuying activity slipped to a new low. Pending home sales fell 0.3% from a week earlier to their lowest level in records dating back to 2021. They declined year over year in every metro we analyzed, with the steepest drops in Seattle (-30.4%), Denver (-26.1%) and San Diego (-24.7%). Higher rates could weigh on demand further in the coming weeks. Total inventory is holding steady. The total number of homes for sale rose 0.2% from a week earlier, while new listings slipped 0.3%. Buyers have leverage. It’s the strongest buyer’s market in records dating back to 2013, per a separate Redfin analysis. There are over half a million more home sellers than buyers throughout the U.S., and just 3 major metros are seller’s markets. House hunters who can afford today’s costs may be able to negotiate with sellers to get a lower price and/or concessions. items.title: Multifamily Permitting’s Share Rebounds as Single-Family Declines
items.description: Multifamily Permitting’s Share Rebounds as Single-Family Declines by Chuck Ehmann Posted November 18, 2026 in Multifamily Construction Permits The share of multifamily permitting to total residential construction has varied greatly over the past sixty-plus years due to either stronger than normal multifamily permitting or weaker single-family construction. From 2000 through 2005, multifamily accounted for only about 18% to 21% of total permits. That was well below the multifamily booms of the 1970s and 1980s, when its share peaked near 47% in 1972 and returned to roughly 37% in 1985. During the 1990s, multifamily permitting averaged about 21% of total housing permits. The early-2000s housing bubble elevated permitting for both segments, but single-family grew faster. That held the multifamily share to about 18% in 2004 before the bust cut permitting for both, with its share bottoming at 14.6% in July 2009. Multifamily recovered faster, and the share has generally exceeded 30% since 2011 as renting as a lifestyle and other societal and economic factors boosted apartment demand. Unusual permitting spikes are evident in the chart ahead of New York’s tax-exempt program changes that pushed the ratio to 45.8% in June 2008 and 46.3% in June 2015. The February 2023 spike of 47.4%, the highest since 1973, came mainly from a slowdown in single-family development as interest and mortgage rates rose, coupled with a post-pandemic surge in multifamily. Single-family permitting recovered somewhat in 2024 and 2025 but has fallen off again recently, pushing the current ratio to 36.7% in October 2026. Seasonally adjusted multifamily permitting was at an annualized rate of 475,000 units in October, down 5.2% for the month and almost unchanged (-0.4%) from last October. Meanwhile, annualized single-family permitting of 772,000 units was down 8.7% from September’s rate and 12.9% from last year. That is the lowest annual rate for single-family since January 2023. The more volatile multifamily starts rate surged 25.5% from September’s revised annual figure to 433,000 units, a 22% increase from last year. September’s reported annual rate was the second lowest in 17 months. Single-family starts increased 4% from last month to 864,000 units but that was 3.2% lower than one year ago. Completions were up for the month for both multi- and single-family homes in October with a 9% increase in multifamily completions to 362,000 and a 6.3% increase in single-family to 900,000 units. However, both were down close to 10% for the year. The number of single-family homes currently under construction was virtually unchanged month-to-month (-0.2%) at 581,000 units, but that annualized rate was down 2.5% from last October. The tally of multifamily units under construction was unchanged from September at 674,000 units and that rate was 3.2% lower than last October. Compared to one year ago, the annual rate for multifamily permitting increased in two of the four regions, with modest improvement in the Northeast (up 3.8% to 76,000 units) and strong growth in the Midwest (up 49.4% to 90,000 units). From 2000 through 2005, multifamily accounted for only about 18% to 21% of total permits.

items.title: Large Median Price Gap Keeps New Homes More Affordable Than Existing Homes
items.description: Large Median Price Gap Keeps New Homes More Affordable Than Existing Homes November 19, 2026 Rose Quint No Comments While housing remains largely unaffordable, a nearly $40,000 gap in the national median price of a new house vs. an existing home kept new construction more affordable relative to existing homes in the third quarter of 2026, according to the latest data from the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB)/Wells Fargo Cost of Housing Index (CHI). The CHI results from the third quarter of 2026 show that a family earning the nation’s median income of $106,800 needed 33% of its income to cover the mortgage payment on a median-priced new home (down from 34% in the second quarter). Low-income families, defined as those earning only 50% of median income, would have to spend 66% (down from 67%) of their earnings to pay for the same new home. The figures are higher for the purchase of existing homes in the U.S. A typical family would have to pay 36% of their income for a median-priced existing home while a low-income family would need to pay 73% of their earnings to make the same mortgage payment. The U.S. data for the percentage of earnings needed to purchase a new home in the third quarter is based on a national median new home price of $393,300, which is down 4.2% from $410,700 in the second quarter. Meanwhile, the corresponding price for an existing home was $432,900 in the third quarter, down 0.5% from $434,900 in the previous quarter. CHI is also available for 175 metropolitan areas, calculating the percentage of a family’s income needed to make the mortgage payment on an existing home based on the local median home price and median income in those markets. In eight out of 175 markets in the third quarter, the typical family is severely cost-burdened (must pay more than 50% of their income on a median-priced existing home). In 87 other markets, such families are cost-burdened (need to pay between 31% and 50%). There are 80 markets where the CHI is 30% of earnings or lower. The Top 5 Severely Cost-Burdened Markets San Jose-Sunnyvale-Santa Clara, Calif., was the most severely cost-burdened market on the CHI, where 79% of a typical family’s income is needed to make a mortgage payment on an existing home. The five most severely cost-burdened markets were: San Jose-Sunnyvale-Santa Clara, Calif. (79%) Urban Honolulu, Hawaii (73%) San Diego-Chula Vista-Carlsbad, Calif. (70%) San Francisco-Oakland-Fremont, Calif. (66%) Barnstable Town, Mass. (61%) Low-income families would have to pay between 122% and 157% of their income in all five of the above markets to cover a mortgage. The Top 5 Least Cost-Burdened Markets By contrast, Decatur, Ill., was the least cost-burdened market on the CHI, where typical families needed to spend just 17% of their income to pay for a mortgage on an existing home. The least cost-burdened markets were: Decatur, Ill. (17%) Elmira, N.Y. (18%) Peoria, Ill. (19%) Wichita Falls, Texas (20%) Springfield, Ill. (20%) Davenport-Moline-Rock Island, Iowa-Ill. (20%) Low-income families in these markets would have to pay between 34% and 41% of their income to cover the mortgage payment for a median-priced existing home. items.description: Pretium Expands Real Estate Debt Platform November 19, 2026 --> Addition of Hilltop Capital Partners Enables the Firm to Deploy Capital to the U.K. Housing Market NEW YORK, November 19, 2026 – Pretium, a specialized investment firm with approximately $70 billion in assets under management, today announced it is expanding its residential real estate debt platform, further enabling the flow of capital to real estate investors, developers, and homebuilders. Since launching its residential debt platform in December 2024, Pretium has lent approximately $8 billion for the purpose of new housing construction and the renovation of existing homes. Building on its existing model, Pretium is adding the team from Hilltop Capital Partners (“Hilltop”), a specialized U.K.-based institutional capital advisor, investment manager and principal lender, to its vertically integrated residential real estate platform. Led by Paul Oberschneider and Tiger Craft, Hilltop has grown into a leading platform for residential development finance across the U.K since its founding in 2019. “The U.K. faces a housing shortage of approximately four to five million homes, and the Hilltop team has built an impressive platform supporting homebuilders, developers and sponsors with flexible, solutions-oriented capital,” said Jonathan Pruzan, Co-President at Pretium. “This expansion is a natural extension of the model we’ve built in the U.S., and we are pleased to welcome the Hilltop team to Pretium. Our real estate debt platform provides much-needed capital to grow the housing stock, while delivering value to our investors.” “U.K. homebuilders need capital that understands development risk and the full ecosystem of finance. Joining the Pretium ecosystem provides us the scale the U.K. homebuilder market requires right now, and I’m excited about what this means for the business in the years ahead,” said Paul Oberschneider, Chairman of Hilltop. "We are thrilled to be joining Pretium. The firm's depth of talent and focus on residential markets make this a natural fit for Hilltop. This gives us the infrastructure and backing to deliver flexible financing to U.K. residential developers and sponsors with greater speed, scale and certainty of execution," said Tiger Craft, CEO of Hilltop. About Pretium Pretium is a specialized investment firm focused on U.S. residential real estate equity and credit. Pretium was founded in 2012 and has built an integrated analytical and operational ecosystem within the U.S. housing and credit markets and believes that its insight and experience within these markets create a strategic advantage. Pretium’s platform has approximately $70 billion in assets and employs 7,000 people across 45+ offices as of June 30, 2026, including its New York headquarters, Miami, London, Abu Dhabi, Bangalore, Seoul and Sydney. Please visit www.pretium.com for additional information. About Hilltop Founded in 2019, Hilltop Credit Partners Limited, trading as Hilltop Capital Partners, is a London-based real estate credit investment adviser and principal lender, focused on providing capital solutions to residential property developers across the UK and Europe. Funds advised by Hilltop have provided c. $300 million in debt funding to support the construction of over 1,000 residential units across the UK. ### Media Contact Brenna Karp Pretium [email protected]

items.description: Houston new-home sales dip to lowest level of 2026 by Emily Marek November 19, 2026 The state of new-home sales in Houston, featuring data from HomesUSA.com. Houston new-home sales declined marginally month over month in October, dipping to the lowest volume of the year so far, according to the Texas New Home Sales Report from HomesUSA.com . Buyers purchased 1,724 new homes during the month, down just slightly from September but down 12.7% from October 2025, when 1,975 new homes sold. Pending sales also declined both monthly and annually. Buyers contracted on 1,447 new homes in October, down 6.2% from 1,542 in September and 17.8% from 1,761 a year prior. Prices decreased monthly as well: The average was $402,169, down 1% from September but up 0.2% from October 2025. “Houston pending sales, a predictor of future sales, peaked five months ago in May and are now at their lowest levels since 2022,” said Ben Caballero , CEO of HomesUSA.com. “New-home sales are also at their lowest levels since 2022. New-home prices are following a similar downward trend.” Meanwhile, days on market increased nine days year over year, but remained essentially flat month over month at 98 days. “Don’t misunderstand what Houston’s days on market is telling us year over year. items.title: Single-family permits telegraph a weakened 2027 building pipeline
items.description: While October saw a blip in housing starts, the latest residential construction data from the U.S. Census Bureau shows a single-family construction market seeking rock bottom, with single-family permits hitting a nearly four-year low. National housing starts rose to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.309 million in October, up 9.9% from the revised September figure of 1.191 million and 2.8% above the same month last year (1.273 million). Most of that increase came from multifamily, where starts climbed 23.6% from September to an annualized rate of 445,000. Single-family starts came in at an annual rate of 864,000 in October, up 4.0% from September but down 3.2% from a year earlier, suggesting single-family construction lacks momentum. "Given monthly volatility, the three-month moving average provides a clearer signal, which fell to 859,000 units," according to a note by National Association of Home Builders Assistant VP for Forecasting and Analysis Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington The future construction pipeline also looks soft. Single-family permits, a forward-looking indicator of where new home construction levels are headed, dropped 8.7% in October to an annual rate of 772,000, down from a revised 846,000 in September and 12.9% lower than a year ago. That marks the lowest level for single-family permits since January 2023. Total housing permits, including both multifamily and single-family, were 8.7% below the October 2025 rate of 1.418 million. “Permits point to a slowdown in single-family production ahead,” First American Chief Economist Mark Fleming said in a provided statement. “Since permits lead construction, the decline suggests builders are moving ahead with projects already in the pipeline, while authorizing fewer single-family homes for future construction.” The new data comes as homebuilder confidence fell to its lowest level in nearly 15 years in November, with affordability constraints and hesitant buyers weighing on the market. That buyer hesitancy is reflected in the latest new home sales figures, which show sales down 5.3% year over year in September and sales prices down roughly 4.0% to $400,400. Fleming pointed to weakening demand, higher costs and elevated mortgage rates as catalysts for a softening residential construction pipeline. “Prospective buyer traffic fell to its weakest level in 15 years, outside the start of the pandemic. Builders are using price cuts and incentives to reach buyers, while labor shortages and higher fuel costs are adding to the cost of building. That combination leaves builders cautious about adding production when affordability is already keeping many buyers on the sidelines,” he said. Homes under construction slip as completions lag The stock of homes under construction continues to move down from recent highs. Housing units under construction totaled 1.27 million in October, 3.0% below a year earlier. Single-family units under construction came to 581,000, down 2.5% year over year, while multifamily units in progress fell to 691,000, 3.5% lower than a year ago and well off the peak of more than 1 million reached in December 2023. Meanwhile, housing completions improved from September but remained negative year on year. Total completions reached an annual rate of 1.272 million in October, up 6.5% from September’s revised 1.194 million but 10.4% below the 1.419 million recorded in October 2025. Single-family completions came in at 900,000, down 10.7% compared to a year earlier, while multifamily completions in buildings with five or more units ran at 362,000, down 9.0% on the year. Regional trends Year to date, combined single-family and multifamily starts rose 3.8% in the Northeast and 0.2% in the South, while falling 0.7% in the Midwest and 6.7% in the West. Single-family construction declined across all four regions, signaling the strain high construction costs and affordability constraints are putting on homebuilders and prospective buyers. The permit data points in the same direction. Total permits are up 8.7% in the Northeast and 2.0% in the Midwest this year, but down 4.4% in the South and 2.5% in the West. With single-family permits lower in all four regions, the outlook for a slowing national construction pipeline looks even more likely. items.title: Housing groups urge FHFA to delay condo reserve rule until 2028
items.description: Five housing and mortgage industry trade groups are asking the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) to delay a planned increase in condominium association reserve requirements by one year, citing implementation challenges and potential financing disruptions. In a Nov. 19 letter sent to FHFA Director Bill Pulte , the organizations asked the agency to direct Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to postpone the changes from Jan. 4, 2027, to Jan. 4, 2028. The new requirement would increase the minimum reserve allocation for applicable condominium project reviews from 10% to 15% of annual budgeted assessment income. The letter was signed by the Community Associations Institute , Community Association Roundtable , Community Home Lenders of America ( CHLA ), Housing Policy Council and National Association of Mortgage Brokers ( NAMB ). The groups said they support adequately funded condominium reserves but argued that associations, lenders and homeowners need more time to prepare for the change. Some have asked for change before. In June, NAMB asked the FHFA to delay upcoming Fannie and Freddie condo review and insurance standards by 12 months. But Fannie Mae retired its limited review process for condominium projects on Aug. 3. "Condominium project eligibility has already declined following recent changes to project review requirements, including the elimination of Limited Review options," the groups wrote. Outlining their concerns The coalition identified three primary concerns with the planned increase, stating that "the change could have unintended consequences for condominium financing and housing availability." First, many condominium associations operate on annual budget cycles and cannot easily adjust their funding midyear. Some may also need updated reserve studies, board approvals or homeowner consultations before changing their funding practices. The groups also said questions remain about how the new requirement will apply to existing budgets, recently completed reserve studies, major capital improvement projects and alternative funding arrangements. Lenders, servicers and condo management companies will also need time to update their systems, underwriting procedures and project reviews. Second, the groups warned that associations unable to meet the higher reserve requirement or qualify under an alternative reserve study provision could lose eligibility for conventional financing through the government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs). The groups raised concerns that this could reduce the pool of potential buyers, make it more difficult for existing homeowners to sell or refinance, and put pressure on condo resale values. The impact could be particularly pronounced in older buildings, smaller communities and associations with more "modest-income" homeowners, the letter stated. Projects that lose conventional financing eligibility could become more reliant on nonagency or portfolio loans, which may be more expensive or less readily available. Lastly, the coalition said higher reserve contributions could add to housing costs at a time when homeowners are already facing elevated mortgage payments, property taxes , insurance premiums, maintenance expenses and association fees. Fannie Mae has estimated that the higher reserve requirement could add an average of $13 to $14 per month to condominium owners' costs, but the actual increase would vary by association, according to the coalition. Its accompanying analysis illustrated how the additional five percentage points could affect homeowners if the entire increase were funded through regular assessments. As part of the proposed one-year extension, the coalition urged FHFA to convene industry stakeholders to evaluate the financial and operational effects of the change, clarify how existing reserve studies and funding arrangements will be treated, and develop transition provisions for associations working toward adequate reserve funding. "We believe that strengthening condominium financial health and maintaining housing affordability should be complementary objectives," the letter said. items.title: Senate committee advances Matt Jones’ nomination as FHA commissioner
items.description: Matt Jones’ nomination to serve as assistant secretary for housing at the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and as Federal Housing Administration (FHA) commissioner advanced in the Senate on Thursday, moving through committee on a narrow vote. The Senate Committee on Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs approved his nomination 13-11, sending it to the full Senate for consideration. Jones would permanently fill the vacancy left by Frank Cassidy in June and succeed Joseph Gormley , who has been serving in the role on an acting basis. Committee chair Tim Scott (R-S.C.) said Jones’ mix of public- and private-sector experience is central to his support. According to Scott, housing affordability remains one of the biggest challenges facing families across America, but if confirmed, Jones “will play an important role in implementing the 21st Century Road to Housing Act and helping more families achieve the American dream of home ownership.” Jones currently serves as HUD’s deputy assistant secretary for single-family housing. He previously was associate vice president of government housing finance at the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), senior adviser for capital markets at A merifirst Home Mortgage , and senior counsel for the Senate’s Finance and Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs committees. The 13-11 vote reflected partisan divisions over the direction of federal housing policy and FHA’s role in addressing affordability and ownership gaps. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), the committee’s ranking member, voted against the nomination, saying Jones’ office has “cut resources for first-time homebuyers and proposed weak rules for keeping foreclosed homes in the hands of families instead of corporations.” “We should vote to make life more affordable for American families. But these nominees will do the opposite, accelerating the Trump administration 's disastrous economic policies,” Warren said. If confirmed, Jones would oversee FHA’s single-family, multifamily and health care mortgage insurance portfolios. FHA currently insures roughly $2 trillion in mortgages. The FHA’s Mutual Mortgage Insurance Fund posted a strong financial performance in fiscal year 2026, even as its capital ratio declined from 2025 levels. The results have renewed industry pressure on FHA to cut annual mortgage insurance premiums to ease costs for first-time and lower-income borrowers. Jones would also inherit an agency that has seen a series of policy adjustments under HUD Secretary Scott Turner , including efforts to revise servicing standards and modernize technology infrastructure. MBA president and CEO Bob Broeksmit said the trade group supports the nomination due to Jones’ “extensive mortgage industry experience, deep understanding of government housing finance, and leadership of FHA’s single-family operations.” “We urge the full Senate to confirm Matt Jones before the 119th Congress adjourns and look forward to working with him and HUD to continue modernizing FHA programs and to improve affordability for owning and renting a home,” Broeksmit said. items.title: Mortgage Rates Surge Again as Stubborn Inflation Ends Brief Reprieve
items.description: Mortgage rates are rising again after four consecutive weeks of declines, as hotter-than-anticipated inflation data sets the stage for another interest rate hike, putting upward pressure on Treasury yields. The average rate on 30-year fixed home loans jumped to 7.28% for the week ending Nov. 19, up 17 basis points from 7.11% recorded the week before, according to Freddie Mac . For perspective, rates averaged 6.26% one year ago. "While prospective borrowers often shop around for a home, they may not always think to do the same for their mortgage, as comparing multiple rate quotes can potentially save them thousands over a loan's lifetime," says Sam Khater , Freddie Mac's chief economist. The October Consumer Price Index (CPI) report came in above expectations last week on both the headline and core measures, all but guaranteeing that the Federal Reserve will raise its benchmark rate to curb inflation at the next Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on Dec. 8. The looming hike, combined with the persistence of the war in Iran, pushed the 10-year Treasury yield back toward 5% this week, putting mortgage rates on an upward trajectory once again. "The debate has shifted from whether the Fed hikes in December to how aggressively it moves," says Realtor.com® senior economist Anthony Smith . "That is a tough backdrop for mortgage rates heading into what is already a seasonally slow stretch for the housing market." Markets are currently pricing a 93% chance of a 25-basis-point increase next month, according to the CME FedWatch tool. Meanwhile, pending home sales fell to a record low in October , and existing home sales hit their lowest level since 2010 , as the surge in mortgage rates through mid-October took its toll on buyers and sellers. Earlier this week, the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) reported builder confidence falling to a new 14-year low, even as permit activity dropped to its lowest level since the early days of the pandemic , signaling that the supply pipeline will face continued pressure in the months ahead. What this means for buyers For buyers who remain active on the market, current conditions offer some meaningful advantages, including less competition from other shoppers, inventory climbing 8.6% year over year, and sellers increasingly willing to negotiate on price. This week, the median listing price fell 2.4% from a year ago to $405,000, matching its steepest decline since early October, according to the latest Realtor.com weekly housing market update. "The challenge is that until inflation cools enough to put mortgage rates on a durable downward path, affordability will remain the dominant constraint on the market," says Smith. Loading... How your credit score affects your mortgage Your credit score plays a role when you apply for a mortgage . A credit score will determine whether you qualify for a mortgage and the interest rate you'll receive. The higher the credit score, the lower the interest rate you'll qualify for. The credit score you need will vary depending on the type of loan. A score of 620 is a "fair" rating. However, people applying for a Federal Housing Administration loan might be able to get approved with a credit score of 500, which is considered a low score. Homebuyers with credit scores of 740 or higher are typically considered to be in very good standing and can usually qualify for better rates, which can reduce monthly payments. items.title: The Ultimate Playbook To Buying a Home Without 20% Down Using Grants and Assistance Programs
items.description: Buying a home can be an intimidating process, with the biggest hurdle for many being coming up with enough funds for a down payment . Many people believe they need to put down at least 20% if they want a home. But that's not necessarily true. Most buyers have down payments ranging from 3.5% to 20% of the sale price of the home they're buying, and there are many down payment assistance programs that can help aspiring homeowners pivot from home browser to homebuyer. These programs can help buyers snag a home by providing cash that can go toward a down payment. There are even loan programs for certain qualified buyers that don't require any down payments. The array of offerings from federal, local, and private sources can take the form of looser loan requirements, outright grants of money, or tax credits, all of which make homeownership more affordable. First-time homebuyers , often with certain qualifications, are often beneficiaries of the assistance. Lower-income buyers, those who serve in the military or are veterans, and those who purchase fixer-uppers or homes in rural areas might also be eligible for the help. The assistance ranges greatly, from a grant of several thousand dollars to, at the high end, a savings of five figures over the life of the loan . What are down payment assistance programs? Down payment assistance can take several forms and can even help buyers circumvent the PMI payment. While 20% down has been something of a gold standard for homebuyers, it's also the minimum that generally lets them avoid private mortgage insurance , or PMI, which is assessed because lenders believe the loan carries risk. This in turn raises the homebuyer’s monthly expenses. Here's an example: PMI is typically 0.5% to 1% of the loan amount per year. So if buyers put down less than 20% and their mortgage is $300,000, their PMI would be between $1,500 and $3,000 per year. That would add about $125 to $250 per month on top of their mortgage payment, a significant charge. (Homeowners can have PMI canceled when the equity in their home surpasses 20%.) So, while a buyer can also choose loans that require a down payment of just a single digit, that PMI can stretch a budget paper-thin. That's where down payment assistance can help. At least 2,000 such programs exist across the country. Some are federal, but most tend to be at state and local levels, which is important to know when searching for help. Private organizations, from lenders to nonprofits, also work with borrowers who need help. These programs might offer grants, loans, tax credits, or a combination of a couple of these benefits. Funding can come from our government, nonprofits, and private enterprises. Let’s take a closer look: Grants might be the most desirable form of down payment assistance. Typically, a grant is fully forgiven at closing and never has to be paid back. Yes, we’re talking about free money! About 7% of down payment help comes in the form of grants, says Veronica Khandelwal , vice president of HFA Relations at Down Payment Resource , which provides consumers with guidance on this kind of assistance. But there is a catch. “Grants require owner occupancy," she says of the requirement for buyers to live in these properties. That's to make sure these loans don't go to investors or vacation-home buyers. "Some programs allow grants to be applied to multifamily purchases of one to four units so long as one of the units is occupied by the borrower." Loading... Forgivable loans are another option. These loans need to be repaid only if a repayment trigger event occurs, such as the home being sold before the end of the term, the home being no longer owner-occupied, the title being transferred, or the loan being defaulted on. Deferred-payment loans are also available. These are paid back either at the end of the loan term or if a repayment trigger occurs. So, while it’s not a gift, it will help homebuyers get over that down payment hurdle and buy a house they might otherwise not have been able to afford. Repayable loans are another leg up on homeownership. They require borrowers to make monthly payments, like a typical loan. But here's the good part: They do so at interest rates starting as low as 0%. That helps spread the down payment and closing costs over a number of years, making it much easier to enter the housing market. Some agencies also offer a combination of these forms of assistance. That could mean that a portion of the help will be forgiven (or “written off” with no repayment needed), while some will need to be repaid. Tax credits are sometimes offered as well, further sweetening the deal. Each down payment assistance program will have its own rules and guidelines, but the vast majority are offered only for a home that buyers will live in as a primary residence. FHA (Federal Housing Authority) loans were created by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development for first-time homeowners (HUD). These mortgages allow as little as 3.5% for the down payment, provided buyers have a credit score of 580 or higher, along with other qualifying factors. The federal government insures these loans, and for that reason, banks are more willing to loan money to homebuyers who have neither top-tier credit nor loads of cash to put down on the purchase. FHA Section 203(k) loans require only 3% down, provided qualifying buyers will live in the property, typically one that needs work, while they fix it up. For buyers hoping for a DIY route into a dream home, this could be a win-win. The cost of improvements is included in the loan so buyers can finance both the home and up to $35,000 in repairs. items.title: Office REIT Sells Reston Property To Local Firm For 30% Of 2014 Price
items.description: Office Properties Income Trust, which emerged from bankruptcy in June, has offloaded a Reston, Virginia, office building for less than a third of its sale price 12 years ago. Google Maps The 135K SF office property at 1775 Wiehle Ave. in Reston, Virginia The REIT, managed by Massachusetts-based The RMR Group, sold the 135K SF property at 1775 Wiehle Ave. — which is just over half vacant — to Bethesda-based Polinger Co. for $12.1M. The sale closed Oct. 22, according to Fairfax County property records. That price is well below what it sold for in 2014, when First Potomac Realty Trust paid $41M for the asset. OPI gained control of the property three years later, when it acquired First Potomac. Polinger likes the supply-and-demand dynamics of the Reston office market, with growing appetite from defense and technology companies and a tightening supply as office parks are converted to residential, John Gordon, president of the firm's development arm, told Bisnow . "We think over the years that the value goes up tremendously because of the lack of new buildings and taking down the buildings and just this great location," he said. OPI did not respond to a request for comment, and a spokesperson for RMR declined to comment on its behalf. OPI is selling off large swaths of its now 16M SF office portfolio. The REIT, like many other office-heavy owners, was hit hard by post-pandemic tidal shifts in office capital markets. The company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October 2025, a year after notifying investors about doubts that it could continue operating in light of its maturing debt. During the restructuring process, OPI shed $714M in debt, leaving it with $1.7B in money owed. At the end of its restructuring, it said it had 31 properties totaling 3M SF on the market that it would sell to repay debts. As of the end of September, the REIT was under agreements to sell 15 office assets totaling more than 1.7M SF, according to its third-quarter report , including one more in Reston and two in Washington, D.C. OPI already sold 13 properties, totaling 1.5M SF, during the third quarter. Those were sold for a total of $143M, and OPI recorded a $5.5M loss on the sales. One of those sales was a 140K SF Dupont Circle office building, which it offloaded for $6.2M in September. On the 1775 Wiehle sale, OPI recorded a $2.3M loss on impairment of real estate. 1775 Wiehle, which was built in 2000, is just under 50% leased, Gordon told Bisnow . The building is anchored by law firm Odin Feldman Pittleman, which has a 35K SF long-term lease at the property, he said. Other tenants include law firm Goel & Anderson and Forge Financial Group. Polinger plans to put money into tenant improvement allowances and build out a full floor of spec suites, in addition to a spec-suite floor added by OPI. The company is seeing interest from medical tenants as well as engineering companies and government contracting firms, Gordon said. Polinger’s website says it manages 3M SF of office, retail and mixed-use space across the D.C. area, including office buildings in the District, Fairfax, Bethesda, Chevy Chase, Gaithersburg and Landover. This summer, the company offloaded a 235K SF Navy Yard office building to Matthew Jemal’s new investment firm, Jemal Equities. The $193.3M price for 99 M St. SE was 43% less than Polinger paid when it bought the property in 2019. For 1775 Wiehle, Newmark represented both sides of the transaction, Kassandra Saridakis, a capital markets managing director for the brokerage, told Bisnow. Jud Ryan, James Cassidy and Grant Marley represented the seller. Saridakis worked with Joe Donato, Andrew Asbill and Kevin Ridgway to arrange acquisition financing for Polinger. items.title: Developer Plans 595 Apartments At Woburn Transit Center
items.description: A plan is moving forward to build hundreds of housing units on a 6-acre site at the Anderson Regional Transportation Center in Woburn. Wikimedia Commons/Pi.1415926535 An aerial view of the Anderson Regional Transportation Center Boston-based developer Cabot, Cabot & Forbes was the sole respondent to Massport 's request for the site, proposing a 595-unit project, Banker & Tradesman first reported . The Massport board of directors unanimously backed the developer's proposal during a Thursday morning meeting. The transportation center includes stops on the MBTA commuter rail's Lowell line and the Amtrak Downeaster line to Maine, and it offers direct bus service to the airport through Logan Express. The site includes nearly 2,400 parking spaces and sits in a 260-acre Superfund site that has contaminants from centuries-old manufacturing. Massport, in partnership with the Massachusetts Department of Transportation and the MBTA, issued a request for expressions of interest in February 2025 to gauge the site's "potential for commercial and residential development to co-exist with, and even enhance, operations at the facility." The project needs approval from all three agencies to move forward. CCF will then need to obtain zoning approval from the city and the Massachusetts Environmental Policy Act Office. CCF has developed another 389-unit project in the Superfund site: The Point at Woburn at 120 Commerce Way. The developer also celebrated the topping off of The Bolt , a 180K SF manufacturing facility on New Boston Street. And Cabot, Cabot & Forbes has proposed another multifamily project called Zero New Boston , a seven-story, 250-apartment complex planned to be built at 0 New Boston St. next to the transportation center. CCF said it has invested roughly $400M in the site. Woburn officials have been trying to reimagine the New Boston Street corridor , hiring RKG Associates to conduct a study on redevelopment and reinvestment opportunities. As part of a March presentation, the city explored several options for reinvestment , including a mixed-use district and a modified industrial zone. items.title: October’s Rate Relief May Not Last, Marcus & Millichap Says
items.description: National CRE News In Your Inbox. Sign up for Connect emails to stay informed with CRE stories that are 150 words or less. National + Weekender | November 19, 2026 By: Amy Wolff Sorter October’s Rate Relief May Not Last, Marcus & Millichap Says October and early November generated some good news for commercial real estate investors. The 10-year Treasury yield fell from about 5.3% on Sept. 29 to 4.8% on Nov. 4. At the same time, September employment data was weaker than expected, while optimism resulting from the mid-term elections “suggested that government could provide some guardrails against policy uncertainty,” said Marcus & Millichap Senior Vice President John Chang in a recently released video . Additionally, investors began moving capital out of AI-related investments and into bonds. Now, for the not-so-good news. “The Fed's dual mandate is maximum employment and stable prices, and the recently released October employment and inflation reports are both pointing toward renewed pressure to raise rates,” chang said. “October offered some interest rate relief, but the forces pushing interest rates higher haven’t gone away,” Chang said. Jobs and Inflation The economy added 165,000 jobs in October, while revisions added another 84,000 positions to August and September, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Unemployment edged down to 4.1%. By Marcus & Millichap’s count, job additions this year totaled 861,000 through October. Yes, the job numbers are often revised lower. Still, “although hiring remains well below historical norms, the employment market is now at its healthiest level in roughly two years, giving the Fed more latitude to tighten policy,” Chang said. Then, there’s inflation, which Chang said is a bigger concern. Last year’s government shutdown left the BLS without October 2025 price data, so there is no official year-over-year inflation rate for October. Marcus & Millichap estimated it at about 4%, which is two times the Fed’s 2% target. Not helping are the price pressures, which Chang said are moving beyond energy and transportation into groceries, restaurants and recreation. “That raises the risk of more entrenched inflation, which is considerably harder for the Fed to control,” Chang explained. The above is prompting markets to price in aggressive Fed action, with investors putting the odds of a 25-bps increase in December at 87% and a 50-bps increase at 13%. At the same time, Marcus & Millichap said the odds that the overnight fed funds rate will reach 4.25% or higher in January have climbed to 69%. “That shift is already putting renewed upward pressure on longer-term treasury yields,” according to Chang. The Impact on CRE Many in the CRE sector have been down this road before. Higher means more expensive debt for acquisitions and refinancing. “For some owners, that will force difficult decisions: cash-in refinance, higher debt payments, the sale of a property, or even giving the keys back to the lender,” Chang said. At the same time, rising rates could create more opportunities, especially as property prices recalibrate and assets facing financial headwinds come to market. “The bottom line: October offered some interest rate relief, but the forces pushing interest rates higher haven't gone away,” Chang said. “But as always, rate trends can be fickle, particularly over the short term.” Photo: Ciprian Alexandru/Shutterstock Read More News Stories About: Marcus & Millichap Connect Inside The Story Marcus & Millichap About Amy Wolff Sorter I love content.
